title: Chrome Extensions Hijacked Search for 13.4 Million Users: What Happened and How to Check Your Browser
desc: Security researchers found 319 extensions that quietly changed the default search engine and sent every query through the operator's servers. What is confirmed, what is not, and a two-minute check.
text: Written on 5 November 2026. The campaign is still being tracked, and researchers keep finding new extensions. Most of the facts below come from the security firm Socket and from reports by BleepingComputer and Malwarebytes. We did not retrieve Socket's own report, so the list of affected extensions is not reproduced here. Use the link in the sources to check it. Socket researcher John Tuckner has documented 319 Chrome extensions that changed the default search engine in users' browsers and sent every search through servers run by the extension's operator before the results appeared. The extensions report a combined 13.4 million installs. Their operators were paid referral fees by Yahoo or Bing for the traffic. It is a search hijack, not a ransomware attack or a stolen password database, and so far there is no public evidence of stolen files or installed malware. It still matters, because a search box is where people type health questions, money worries and workplace problems. This article sets out what was found, what the extensions could and could not do, and how to check your own browser in about two minutes. The short version Socket found 319 extensions with about 13.4 million reported installs. BleepingComputer reported the findings on 29 October 2026. The new report builds on Tuckner's April 2025 finding of 57 extensions with 6 million users. It adds 264 extensions and about 8.7 million users. The extensions replaced the default search engine and routed queries through the operator's proxy before sending them to Bing or Yahoo. The operators earned referral payments. They were disguised as PDF converters, manual finders, "safe search" tools and "AI search" tools, and were promoted through ads. Socket did not find evidence that searches were redirected to phishing or malware pages. It warns that the destination could change at any time. The 13.4 million figure is a cumulative total over roughly a decade, not the number of people affected this week. Check chrome://extensions and the default search engine setting. Instructions are below. What the researchers found In April 2025 Tuckner described 57 extensions with about 6 million users that behaved this way. The October 2026 report widens the picture. It adds 264 extensions with about 8.7 million users, for a total of 319 and 13.4 million. BleepingComputer describes two large clusters. One, labelled "Bing-Search", has 37 extensions and about 2.2 million users and was often promoted through ads from a network called Bidbrain. The other, "SecuryBrowse", has 58 extensions and about 4.9 million users, and uses security-themed names such as Fire Shield, Securify and WatchTower. Most of the extensions had already been removed from the Chrome Web Store by the time of publication. New ones keep appearing. BleepingComputer asked Google for comment and had not received a reply when it published. How the hijack worked A single manifest setting Chrome lets an extension declare a replacement search provider through a manifest field called chrome_settings_overrides. The field exists for legitimate search tools. The campaign used it as the whole attack. Socket noted that one example had only a manifest and icons, with no background scripts, no content scripts and no requested permissions. An extension like that can look harmless in a review of what it is allowed to do. The detour Once the extension is installed, a search typed in the address bar goes first to a server controlled by the operator. That server passes the query on to Bing or Yahoo, tagged with a partner identifier that tells the search engine whom to pay. Tuckner ties the revenue to a syndication partner ID, which is how these referral programs normally track traffic. In one of his tests, an extension called Predator Search sent six identical searches to four different places: Yahoo with partner tags, a landing page on searchlio.net, a chain through searchtosearch.com to another domain, and a Cloudflare error page. The same search did not always lead to the same result. How people ended up installing them The extensions presented themselves as PDF converters, manual finders, safe-search tools and AI search tools. Most were unlisted in the Chrome Web Store, which means they did not appear in store search results and could only be installed through a direct link. Ads sent people to those links. Malwarebytes says the ads ran on networks that include Google Ads. What the risk actually is Malwarebytes quotes Socket on the main risk: the operators could see what users searched for. Queries were often tied to a unique identifier, which would let an operator link searches from the same browser over time. A person's searches can reveal medical concerns, finances and workplace issues. The second risk is the destination. Because the redirect sits on the operator's server, the page a user lands on can change without any extension update. Socket said it did not find evidence that the extensions had sent users to phishing or malware sites. It treats the behaviour as closer to a potentially unwanted program than to malware, but says the risk of malware remains. Claim What the reporting supports 13.4 million people were infected Not quite. It is the combined reported install count over about a decade, not the number of people newly affected this week. The extensions stole passwords No such finding has been reported. The extensions saw search queries Yes. Queries went through operator-controlled servers. Users were sent to malware pages Socket found no evidence of it, but the destination could be changed at any time. The problem is over No. Many of the listed extensions are gone, but new ones keep appearing. How to check your browser Malwarebytes recommends three checks. They take a few minutes and work the same way in other Chromium-based browsers, with a different address at the start. Review your extensions. Type chrome://extensions in the address bar. In Microsoft Edge the address is edge://extensions, and in Brave it is brave://extensions. Remove anything you do not recognise, no longer use or do not trust. If you are unsure about one, compare it with the list at the end of Socket's report. Check your search engine. Open the three-dot menu, choose Settings, then Search engine, and confirm the default is the one you picked. If the page says an extension controls this setting, open that extension and remove it. Run a security scan. Use an antivirus or anti-malware tool you already trust to look for other unwanted software. Do not treat a missing warning as proof of safety. Malwarebytes points out that the absence of a notice about an extension controlling a setting does not mean your extensions are clean. Signs that something changed Your default search engine changed and you did not change it. Results look unfamiliar, or a search leads to a site you did not expect. The extension list contains tools you do not remember installing. You installed a "PDF", "manual" or "safe search" tool after clicking an ad. Habits that reduce the risk Treat an ad for an extension as a warning sign. The campaign relied on advertising. A legitimate tool rarely needs it. Install only what you use. Each extension is code that runs inside your browser with access you granted once and may have forgotten. Look at the publisher, the install history and the reviews, and remember that a tool can sit in the official store for a long time before it is removed. Review your extension list and default search engine every few months. The two screens above take a minute. Keep work and personal browsing apart. A separate browser profile for work and money limits what a single bad extension can see. The reasons are covered in the profiles guide. Know who can see your searches. The same logic applies to proxies and VPN services. The proxy and VPN comparison explains what each one can and cannot hide. Where Rapid+ fits We build Rapid+ Browser, so the relevant fact is plain. Rapid+ for Android and Windows does not run browser extensions. This kind of hijack cannot arrive through an extension store because the feature does not exist. That is a limit as well as a protection, since you cannot add the tools that extensions provide. The search engine is set in Settings, and a change there is made by you. Rapid+ also has a built-in ad and tracker blocker, so there is less reason to install a separate blocking extension. None of this replaces the habits above on the computers and browsers where you do use extensions. Frequently asked questions How many Chrome extensions were involved? Socket researcher John Tuckner documented 319 extensions with about 13.4 million reported installs. That includes 57 extensions from his April 2025 report and 264 newly identified ones. What did the extensions do? They replaced the browser's default search engine and sent searches through servers controlled by the operator before passing them to Bing or Yahoo. The operators earned referral payments for the traffic. Were passwords or files stolen? No theft of passwords or files has been reported. Socket says it found no evidence that searches were redirected to phishing or malware pages, though the redirect could be changed at any time. Does this affect browsers other than Chrome? The extensions were found in the Chrome Web Store. Other Chromium-based browsers, such as Edge and Brave, can install Chrome extensions, so it is sensible to check the extension list there too. Reports in this campaign focus on Chrome. I removed the extension. Is my browser clean? Check that the default search engine is back to the one you chose and run a scan with a security tool you trust. Search results that still look unfamiliar are a reason to look further. Sources BleepingComputer: Chrome extensions with 13.4 million installs caught hijacking searches (29 Oct 2026) Malwarebytes: Fake PDF and search tools hijacked searches for 13.4 million Chrome users (Oct 2026) eSecurity Planet: Researchers uncover 319 Chrome extensions hijacking search traffic Gridinsoft: Searchjacked, hidden Chrome extensions put a proxy between you and search browsers.to: This week in browsers (1 Nov 2026) Socket's own report (the full extension list) is linked from the BleepingComputer and Malwarebytes articles above. title: How Wars Cut the Internet: What Iran and Russia Show, and What Actually Helps
desc: Iran spent 88 days almost fully offline and Russia switches off mobile internet region by region. Here is what happened, what a VPN can and cannot do, and what you can prepare.
text: Written on 4 November 2026. Rules on the internet change often in countries at war. The newest reporting we could find on Iran is from mid-October, and on Russia from the spring. Treat the numbers below as a snapshot, and check the live trackers listed in the sources before you rely on them. When a war starts, the first thing many people try is to message their family. In Iran on 28 February 2026, that stopped working. On the day the strikes began, the monitoring group NetBlocks measured the country's connection to the outside internet at about 4 percent of normal. About a week later it was around 1 percent. The country stayed cut off for 88 days. Wartime internet cuts are not new, but 2026 has shown how complete they can get, and how different governments use them. Iran switched much of its population off. Russia switches off mobile internet region by region, saying it is a response to Ukrainian drones, and slowly squeezes the tools people use to get around blocks. This article explains what happened in both countries, what a VPN or proxy can and cannot do in each case, and what ordinary people can prepare in advance. The short version Iran's blackout that began with the strikes on 28 February lasted 88 days. NetBlocks called it the longest nationwide internet shutdown in modern history. Partial restoration began on 26 May, and social media stayed blocked. Iran's officials now say more restrictions are possible if the war escalates. They have also described a "tiered" system where some groups, such as traders, researchers and journalists, would keep international access. In Russia, authorities cut mobile internet in many regions, citing the threat of Ukrainian drones, and keep a growing list of approved websites that still work during cuts. A VPN or proxy cannot work if the whole connection is switched off. It can help when specific sites or apps are blocked, until the blockers learn to spot it. Using circumvention tools or satellite equipment can be illegal or dangerous in some countries. Know your local law before you decide. Three different things people call "an internet shutdown" News reports use one phrase for several different problems, and the fix for each is different. What it is What you see Does a VPN help? Full shutdown Almost nothing connects to the outside world. Domestic services may still work. No. A VPN needs a working connection to reach its server. Filtering The internet works, but certain sites and apps are blocked. Often, until the blocking system learns to recognise the VPN. Whitelisting or throttling Only approved services load, or everything is very slow. Only if the VPN's own traffic is on the approved list, which is rare. Most of the confusion comes from mixing these up. Advice that works against filtering, such as "install a VPN", does nothing in a full shutdown. Iran: from protests to war What happened, and when Iran's year of disruption began before the war. During nationwide protests in January, authorities cut access for about three weeks, according to Al Jazeera. When the war began, the internet went down again. When What happened 8 January Nationwide internet and phone blackout during protests. NetBlocks confirms the country is almost fully offline. Late January Access relaxes, but most users are limited to a list of approved sites. 28 February US and Israeli strikes on Iran begin. NetBlocks reports connectivity at about 4 percent of ordinary levels. 6 March Traffic is about 1 percent of normal. April A ceasefire takes effect on 8 April, but the shutdown continues. Around 21 April, authorities begin restoring access to "favoured groups". 25 to 26 May The president orders the blackout ended. NetBlocks confirms partial restoration on day 88, after about 2,093 hours. Late May onward Fixed broadband returns first and mobile networks in stages. Foreign social media stays blocked. The timeline above follows the Wikipedia summary of the blackout and the NetBlocks and Al Jazeera reporting it cites. The dates of the ceasefire are described differently in different sources, and Al Jazeera notes that fighting later eased but that there is still no permanent ceasefire. What it cost NetBlocks estimated the economic loss at up to $37 million a day, and about $1.8 billion in total by mid-April. Iran's communications minister gave a similar figure of $35.7 million a day. These are estimates, not audited numbers, but both the monitor and the government are in the same range. The human cost is harder to count. Families abroad could not reach relatives, including over the Nowruz holiday. Because Iran has no official public alert system, a crowdsourced app called Mahsa Alert was used to share missile warnings. Human rights groups including Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch have said the blackout hid violence during the crackdown on protesters. The government says it limits the internet to protect national systems from cyberattacks, and a spokesperson told reporters in October, "We don't deny this issue." Where it stands now The newest reporting is about satellite internet. Starlink is outlawed in Iran. According to Al Jazeera, using or owning a terminal carries a sentence of six months to two years, importing or distributing them up to five years, and the death penalty is possible if national security or espionage charges are added. Officials call Starlink a "tool of war" and say they have systems to cut off terminals. On 4 October, Iran summoned the Norwegian ambassador over the service. Officials also say more restrictions are possible if the war intensifies. The secretary of the Supreme National Cyberspace Council has backed tiered access, with protected international connections for selected groups. When a version of the idea was proposed in April, students and creators publicly called it discriminatory. A governance framework released in October says some platforms could be unblocked in future, but gives no timeline. Russia: switching off by region, and narrowing the exits Russia's approach looks different. There is no single national blackout. The reporting here comes mostly from Mediazona, an independent outlet, and much of it rests on residents' accounts rather than measurements. Regional mobile shutdowns. Authorities say they are a response to Ukrainian drones. Reports name regions including Omsk, Tyumen, Arkhangelsk, Rostov-on-Don, Bryansk and Krasnodar. Moscow's mobile internet was out for nearly three weeks in March, according to The Bell, which cited the FSB as the body that ordered base stations switched off. In February the State Duma passed a bill that lets the FSB demand shutdowns without the earlier condition of a security threat. A list of approved services. A "registry of socially significant services" was introduced in September 2025 with 57 websites. It includes state media, banks, government services and Russian apps such as VK, Yandex and the state-backed messenger Max. These keep working when ordinary internet is cut. Pressure on VPNs. Apple has removed VPN apps from its Russian App Store almost monthly. Mobile operators were told to charge for international mobile traffic above 15 GB a month from 1 May. Big Russian companies were told to block users who connect through a VPN or risk losing their place on the approved list. Messaging apps. Calls on Telegram and WhatsApp were restricted from August 2025, and tougher limits on Telegram were announced in February 2026. The day-to-day effects described to Mediazona are small and practical. Taxis could not be ordered, bus-tracking apps stopped, and in Bryansk many shops stopped accepting card payments. The article also says shutdowns do not appear to stop the drone strikes they are meant to prevent, and that the military has been frustrated by disrupted communications. That is the outlet's reading, not an official statement. What a VPN or proxy can and cannot do How blocking works Networks block in layers. They can remove a site's name from the directory that turns names into addresses (DNS). They can block the server addresses themselves. And they can inspect the traffic and block anything that looks like a known VPN, a method called deep packet inspection. Mediazona reports that the blocking of one VPN protocol in late 2025 was patchier than first claimed, and that most providers answered with new configurations. It is a game of catch-up, and it is why a tool that works one week may not work the next. When there is no connection at all In a full shutdown, the problem is not a blocked website. The link to the outside world is cut. A VPN, a proxy or a different browser cannot create a connection that is not there. Only a different physical route can, such as satellite, and in Iran that route carries serious legal risk. Three things to be careful about Fake VPN apps. When blocking increases, demand for VPNs jumps and so does the number of fake ones. Proton's censorship tracker, which is published by a VPN company and measures against an undefined baseline, reports surges of hundreds or thousands of percent in VPN use in countries during shutdowns and crackdowns, including Iran and Russia. Treat its figures as signs of demand, not exact measurements. Install any such tool only from its maker's own official page or a trusted app store. Free and unknown servers. A proxy or VPN operator can see the sites you visit and any unencrypted traffic. A server you do not know is a risk, not just a convenience. Legal risk. The law differs by country and changes quickly. This article is not advice to break any law. What ordinary people can prepare before a cut Most of what helps is not about software tricks. It is about what you have ready if the connection drops for days. Agree a plan with family. Decide in advance who contacts whom, at what time, and by which fallback, such as a regular phone call or SMS if those still work. Save the essentials offline. Download offline maps for your area, keep key phone numbers on paper, and save copies of important documents on your device. Know your local alert channels. Many countries send emergency alerts by SMS or cell broadcast, which can work when apps do not. Keep your apps and system updated, and install software only from official sources. Do this before a crisis, not during one. Keep sensitive accounts apart. A separate browser profile for banking and email keeps those logins away from everything else. The profiles guide explains how. If you are abroad and cannot reach someone, keep calls short and avoid pushing relatives to take risks to get online. Rely on verified news sources and not on forwarded messages. Where Rapid+ fits, and where it does not We build Rapid+ Browser, so here is the honest version. Rapid+ has a proxy and VPN mode that sends a profile's traffic through a SOCKS5 or HTTP proxy server that you provide. We do not run proxy servers or sell access. It cannot restore a connection that has been cut, and it does not make you anonymous. An HTTP proxy can read unencrypted traffic, and whoever runs the server can see where you go. It may help with filtering if you already have a proxy you trust and it is legal to use where you are. Rapid+ for Windows 1.3 also has a WebRTC setting that hides your real IP address from websites when you use a proxy, and a time zone setting. The matching options arrive on Android in the next update. None of this is a promise of safety in a country that actively hunts for circumvention tools. Frequently asked questions Can a VPN work during a total internet shutdown? No. A VPN needs an internet connection to reach its server. If the country's link to the outside world is cut, the VPN has nothing to connect through. It only helps when the connection works but certain sites or apps are blocked. What is the difference between a shutdown, filtering and a whitelist? A shutdown cuts most or all connections to the outside internet. Filtering lets the internet work but blocks specific sites and apps. A whitelist allows only approved services and leaves everything else unreachable. Why do governments cut the internet in wartime? Officials usually say they are protecting national systems from cyberattacks or preventing drone attacks. Human rights groups say the cuts also hide abuses and stop people sharing information. Both claims exist in the reporting above, and we cannot independently verify either. Is it legal to use a VPN? It depends on the country, and the rules change. In some places VPNs are legal but certain uses are not, and in Iran, for example, Starlink terminals are outlawed with heavy penalties. Check the law where you are before you decide. How can I check whether a country's internet is being cut? Public trackers publish live measurements. NetBlocks, Cloudflare Radar, OONI and the Access Now campaign against shutdowns are the common ones. They measure different things, so compare more than one. title: The Binance Hack: What Happened, What Was Lost, and What It Means for You
desc: Binance says about $6.3 billion was taken, the largest crypto theft on record. Here is what is confirmed, what is only reported, and what nobody knows yet.
text: Developing story. This was written on 1 November 2026 with the information available that day. Several figures are still preliminary and will change as analysts finish tracing the money. Binance has promised a detailed technical report, and this article is best read alongside it once it is published. On the evening of Thursday 29 October 2026, UTC, money started leaving Binance's wallets faster than anyone could react. Within hours the world's largest crypto exchange had paused withdrawals, its founder was telling people on X that the company had probably been hacked, and analysts were counting a loss that Binance itself put at about $6.3 billion. If that figure holds, it is the biggest theft in the history of cryptocurrency. Elliptic, a blockchain analysis firm, calls it "almost certainly the largest single theft of any kind in history." Two days on, the picture is clearer but far from complete. The FBI has named the group it believes is responsible. Binance says it has already replaced most of what was taken. Roughly half of the stolen value has been frozen. The question engineers care about most, how a company with that much security spending lost control of its wallets, has only a partial answer. This article keeps three layers apart: what Binance has confirmed, what outside analysts and officials have reported, and what nobody knows yet. The short version Binance estimates about $6.3 billion in assets was affected. Independent estimates range from about $5.9 billion to $6.43 billion. Around $3 billion has been frozen, mostly stablecoins. Elliptic independently verified about $2.85 billion. Binance's first explanation was a compromised laptop belonging to a DevOps engineer. It later said there were additional points of breach and has not described them. On 31 October the FBI said North Korea's TraderTraitor group was responsible. Binance says it will absorb the loss, reports replacing about 90 percent of the stolen amount, and planned to reopen withdrawals in stages on 1 November. No reporting so far says customer personal data was taken. What happened, and when Times are UTC. Most of the on-chain detail comes from Elliptic's reconstruction. The statements come from Binance and from news coverage. Binance has not yet published its own timeline. When What happened 28 to 29 Oct An attacker-controlled wallet receives three small withdrawals (0.1 ETH each) from Tornado Cash, a mixing service. The attacker's sweeper contract is rehearsed on another wallet about four hours before the attack. Thu 29 Oct, about 20:05 Five Binance wallets on the XRP Ledger send 233 million XRP to one attacker address. Hot wallets on the other chains follow over roughly the next half hour. 29 Oct, 20:20 to 20:24 On Ethereum, one transaction carries 50 authorizations tied to a Binance hot wallet that Elliptic calls "Binance 14". Minutes later the attacker's contract empties it of 167,464 ETH and 63 tokens, including about 1.6 billion USDT. 29 Oct, about 21:00 Tether freezes the attacker's main Ethereum wallet, locking about $1.18 billion in USDT. Circle freezes about $823 million in USDC. 29 Oct Binance tells reporters it is investigating a potential security issue and suspends withdrawals on multiple networks. Founder Changpeng Zhao posts that the company likely was hacked. 30 Oct Binance publishes a preliminary finding: a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, no evidence of a leaked wallet key, about $6.3 billion affected and about $3 billion frozen. TRM Labs and Chainalysis point to North Korea. The attacker sells stolen AVAX and bridges the proceeds to Ethereum. 30 Oct, later Co-CEO Richard Teng calls it a "complex attack" and says the attackers used malicious software built to delete evidence. Sat 31 Oct The FBI, with the Secret Service and IRS Criminal Investigation, names TraderTraitor and asks crypto businesses to block addresses the group uses. Binance says it has replaced 90 percent of the stolen amount and publishes a new proof of reserves snapshot. Sun 1 Nov Binance plans a staged reopening of withdrawals from 06:00 to 09:00 UTC across 15 networks, starting with Bitcoin, Ethereum, BNB Chain and Solana, according to reports. At the time of writing, we could not confirm it had happened. Speed is the first thing that stands out. Elliptic counts movements across 11 blockchains in about three hours, and the largest single sweep, the Ethereum hot wallet, took roughly three and a half minutes once the attacker's contract was in place. Tether's freeze landed about 40 minutes after that. By then most of the damage was done. How the attack appears to have worked What Binance has said Binance's own first explanation, posted on X, is that the incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which let an attacker reach a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. It added that it had found no evidence of a leaked wallet private key. A DevOps engineer builds and runs the systems that other software runs on, so their laptop tends to hold credentials for servers and deployment tools. A service container is a packaged program running on one of those servers. The withdrawal service is the part of an exchange that takes a customer's request, builds the blockchain transaction and gets it signed from a hot wallet. A hot wallet is one connected to the internet so payouts can happen in seconds. If an attacker can reach a service that already has the authority to sign, they do not need to steal the keys. They ask the machine to sign for them. One reading that fits Binance's statement is exactly that. Elliptic's analysis points the same way: it describes abuse of Binance's own signing systems and sees a resemblance to the Bybit theft of February 2025. What the blockchain shows Elliptic's reading of the Ethereum data adds a detail. A feature called EIP-7702 lets an ordinary wallet hand control to a smart contract. The attacker used it: a single transaction carried 50 authorizations linked to a Binance hot wallet, after which a sweeper contract the attacker had written could drain the wallet in minutes. Elliptic quotes Teng saying the use of that feature "did not pass through our normal approval controls." The same report says a second Binance wallet, "Binance 16", sent about $174 million directly to the attacker, and that the attacker used a wallet's owner rights to pull 823 million USDC out of another one. What is still unknown The laptop was probably not the whole story. Binance has since said there were additional points of breach, and Teng said the attack "was not carried out by one person," according to Elliptic. Nobody outside Binance knows how the approval controls were bypassed, how long the attacker had access, or what the other points of breach were. The promised post-mortem is the document to wait for. How much was taken, and how much was frozen The amounts Elliptic's breakdown of what left Binance, at prices when it was taken: Network Taken Ethereum and Ethereum-based tokens about $3.80 billion across 186 tokens, including about 1.9 billion USDT and 823 million USDC Bitcoin 18,270 BTC, about $1.48 billion Tron 612.7 million USDT XRP Ledger 233 million XRP Total about $6.43 billion You will see several totals in the news, and they are not contradictions so much as different ways of counting: Binance: about $6.3 billion, its own estimate. Elliptic: $6.43 billion. It counts transfers from Binance to the attacker at the time of theft, and leaves out $169 million that left Binance after withdrawals were paused, which went to long-established addresses and looks like Binance moving its own funds. Chainalysis: roughly $5.9 billion at the time of the theft, as reported by CoinDesk. Early reports: "at least $2 billion" and then $5.7 to $5.8 billion. BleepingComputer's figure of up to $5.8 billion was a total of wallet holdings, not a confirmed loss. Dollar values also drift because the stolen assets are priced in a market that fell on the news. Treat every number here as preliminary. The frozen part Binance says about $3 billion has been frozen, including $2.3 billion in the stablecoins USDT and USDC. Elliptic verified $2.85 billion frozen or seized on-chain, 44 percent of the theft, and 94 percent of that was stablecoins on Ethereum and Tron. Tether's chief executive said it froze more than $1.57 billion, and Circle's said it froze more than $800 million. Optimism and Arbitrum secured all of the stolen funds on their networks through governance, and Aave froze the affected markets, according to Elliptic. Stablecoins freeze easily because a company stands behind each one. The issuer's contract can blacklist an address so that its tokens cannot move. Bitcoin and ether have no issuer. They can only be stopped if an exchange, bridge or other service in the path agrees to refuse the funds. That is why the unfrozen remainder, which Elliptic puts at about $3.21 billion and which includes 18,270 BTC and more than 519,000 ETH, is the part to worry about. Where the rest is going Elliptic's tracing shows an attacker in a hurry. About $786 million of stablecoins was swapped into ETH and TRX before freezes landed. One batch of 434 million USDT was converted to ETH at an implied loss of 12 to 26 percent, a haircut the attacker evidently accepted for speed. The bitcoin was split through a peel chain, a series of transfers that each peel a chunk off a large balance, into 19 addresses, mostly 1,000 BTC each. None had reached an exchange or other service at the time of Elliptic's report. The pace looks automated. The main Tron laundering wallet made 546 transfers from 30 October, with a median gap of 96 seconds. Chainalysis chief executive Jonathan Levin said the attackers had already used thousands of addresses and that the count could reach tens of thousands in the coming weeks as the money moves through bridges, instant exchanges and swappers. The FBI said the actors were mainly converting the haul into ether and expects them to keep laundering it in stages. Who is blamed, and how sure anyone is The attribution has two layers. The first is analyst judgment. TRM Labs assessed with high confidence that TraderTraitor, a North Korean state hacking unit linked to the Lazarus Group, was behind it, and Chainalysis and Elliptic reached the same view. Elliptic listed its evidence: the stolen funds are being laundered alongside proceeds of a September 2026 exploit of the exchange Bitget that it assessed as likely North Korean, the same services appear in three earlier TraderTraitor thefts, the preparation was long and appeared to target staff, and the abuse of signing systems resembles Bybit. It also argued that very few groups could coordinate across 11 chains in about three hours. The second layer is official. On 31 October the FBI said North Korea's TraderTraitor was responsible, the same group it blamed for the $1.5 billion Bybit theft. It urged crypto businesses to block transactions tied to the laundering and shared more than 600 Ethereum addresses, just under 20 Bitcoin addresses and one Solana address. What is still open: the FBI has not published the evidence behind its conclusion, and Binance has not described the attackers itself. The attribution is strong. The details of the intrusion are not yet public. What it means if you have money on Binance What Binance says Binance says customer funds are safe and that it will cover the loss. Its words: "Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users." It reports funding the replacement from its Secure Asset Fund for Users, known as SAFU, which holds about $1 billion in bitcoin, part of a futures insurance fund, and corporate money. SAFU alone could not cover $6.3 billion, so company money is doing most of the work. By Saturday Binance said it had replaced 90 percent of the stolen amount by buying new tokens, with the remainder mostly in less liquid assets it was still buying. Crypto Briefing reported that its ten most-held assets, including BTC, ETH, USDT, BNB and SOL, were fully covered. Later reports put overall replacement at about 95 percent, a figure that so far appears only in secondary coverage. What you can check Binance published a new proof of reserves snapshot at 00:00 UTC on 31 October, and outlets report a more detailed verification expected on 2 or 3 November. A proof of reserves compares the wallets an exchange controls against what it owes customers, and lets you confirm your own balance is counted. It is a useful signal, but it is not an audit and it says little about other debts. Treat it as one input. The market Bitcoin fell about 5 percent to below $77,000, ether about 5.7 percent, BNB about 8 percent and Aave about 11 percent, according to CoinDesk. DefiLlama put Binance's assets at roughly $144 billion before the theft, so the stolen amount is around 4 percent of that. Macquarie University's Sean Foley, quoted by Al Jazeera, said that "Any assets held at a centralised exchange are only as safe as the exchange itself." This article does not tell you whether to withdraw, hold or buy. It can tell you what is known, and a lot of it is still Binance's word. What about personal data? Nothing in the coverage so far says customer personal data, such as ID documents used for verification or email addresses, was accessed. Binance's statements are about wallets and funds. Read that as not reported, not as ruled out. If customer data was involved, the post-mortem is where it should show up. Binance has denied claims of leaked customer data in the past, including an alleged breach it said did not come from its systems, and those older claims are unrelated to this incident. The more immediate data risk is scams. Binance warned users to distrust unofficial links and messages asking for account details. News like this reliably triggers phishing: texts and emails claiming your withdrawal was cancelled, your account is locked, or you are owed compensation. In 2022 CoinDesk reported Binance's then chief executive warning about a text-message campaign built around a link to cancel a withdrawal, which led to a page that harvested logins. How it compares with earlier hacks Incident Amount Notes Binance (2026) about $6.3 billion (Binance), $6.43 billion (Elliptic) FBI blames TraderTraitor Bybit (2025) about $1.4 to $1.5 billion FBI and analysts blame TraderTraitor; a planned transfer was manipulated Ronin Network (2022) roughly $550 to $620 million, depending on prices Validator keys; US Treasury tied it to Lazarus BNB Chain bridge (2022) $570 million minted, about $100 million actually taken Chain was paused Poly Network (2021) about $611 million Nearly all returned within two weeks Coincheck (2018) about $530 million in NEM More than 260,000 users; about $400 million refunded Binance (2019) about 7,000 BTC, over $40 million One hot wallet; covered from SAFU Elliptic says the Binance theft is more than four times the size of Bybit and more than six times the roughly $1 billion taken from the Central Bank of Iraq in 2003. It also says the haul almost doubles what North Korea is believed to have stolen over the years, which it puts at more than $6.5 billion before this incident. TRM's 2026 report counted $2.87 billion stolen in nearly 150 hacks during all of 2025. Binance's own 2019 theft is a useful contrast. Then, hackers used phishing, viruses and stolen API keys and two-factor codes against a hot wallet holding about 2 percent of its funds, and SAFU covered the loss. This time the same fund is a fraction of what was needed. One laptop, six billion dollars Exchanges spend heavily on cold storage, approval workflows and hardware security. The reported way in was still a single employee's computer. That is the pattern in many large breaches: the strongest lock does not matter if someone can be handed the key, or a machine that already holds it can be made to act. Bybit's 2025 loss came from a manipulated transfer rather than a cracked wallet, and Ronin's from compromised validator keys. Your own setup is smaller, but the principle scales down. Your laptop or phone holds your email, your password manager, your exchange login and an open browser session. Malware that can read a page can use a logged-in account without ever learning the password, and two-factor codes do not help once a session has been hijacked. The device is the weak point more often than the algorithm. Protecting your own accounts None of this requires special skill. These are the habits that would have helped in the incidents above. Expect scams this week. Do not click links in texts or emails about the hack. Open the exchange's app or type the address yourself. Set an anti-phishing code in your account if the exchange offers one, so genuine emails carry it. Use passkeys or a hardware security key instead of SMS codes. SIM swapping and text interception are old and still effective. Turn on a withdrawal address whitelist and, where offered, a delay. An attacker who gets into your account then cannot send funds to a new address immediately. Revoke API keys you do not use and log out other sessions. Stolen API keys and two-factor codes were part of Binance's 2019 theft. Do not leave everything on an exchange. A balance there is a promise from a company. Holding your own keys has risks of its own, because losing a recovery phrase loses the funds, so decide with your eyes open. If you buy a hardware wallet, buy it from the maker. Never type a recovery phrase into a website or app, and ignore anyone who asks for it, including "support". Keep finance in its own browser profile with no extensions you do not need, a bookmarked exchange address, and an operating system and browser that are up to date. A separate profile keeps your shopping and social logins away from it. The reasons are covered in the profiles guide. Check the address bar every time. Look-alike domains and sponsored search ads are how many people reach fake exchange sites. Read proof of reserves reports with their limits in mind. They show one moment in time, and they are not a statement of everything an exchange owes. Frequently asked questions How much was stolen from Binance? Binance estimates about $6.3 billion in assets was affected. Elliptic puts the figure at about $6.43 billion and Chainalysis at roughly $5.9 billion at the time of the theft. The totals are preliminary and move with crypto prices. About $3 billion has been frozen. Is my money on Binance safe? Binance says user funds are safe and that it will absorb the loss. It reports replacing about 90 percent of the stolen assets and has published a new proof of reserves snapshot. Those are Binance's own statements, and a fuller independent check is still pending. This article is not financial advice. Who hacked Binance? The FBI said on 31 October 2026 that North Korea's TraderTraitor group, which is part of the wider Lazarus Group, was responsible. Private analysts at TRM Labs, Chainalysis and Elliptic had reached the same assessment earlier. Binance has not described the attackers itself. Was my personal data leaked? No reporting so far says customer personal data, such as ID documents or email addresses, was accessed in this incident. That means not reported, which is different from proven absent. Binance's technical post-mortem is where it should be settled. When can I withdraw again? Binance planned to reopen withdrawals in stages on 1 November 2026, starting with networks including Bitcoin, Ethereum, BNB Chain and Solana, and said exact timing could shift after security checks. Check Binance's official channels for the current status. Can the stolen money be recovered? Part of it has been frozen already, about $3 billion by Binance's count and $2.85 billion by Elliptic's verification, mostly stablecoins. The rest includes bitcoin and ether, which no company can freeze, and it is being moved through swaps and bridges. In the 2022 Ronin theft, which the US Treasury tied to Lazarus, only about $30 million was recovered, according to Decrypt. A note on Rapid+ Rapid+ Browser lets you keep a profile just for banking and crypto, with its own cookies and logins, on Android and Windows. It will not protect you from malware on your device, which is the lesson of this story: a browser is one layer, not the whole defense. Details are on the multiple profiles page. title: Browser Fingerprinting: How Websites Recognize You Without Cookies
desc: Nothing is stored on your device, so there is nothing to clear. Here is what fingerprinting measures, how well it works in practice, and what helps.
text: Clearing your cookies used to be the way to start fresh with a website. It still matters, but it is no longer the whole story. A fingerprinting script can recognize your browser by measuring it: the screen size, the fonts you have installed, your graphics hardware, your time zone and language, and small differences in how your machine draws text and processes sound. Nothing is saved on your device, so there is nothing to delete. This article explains what a fingerprint is made of, what the research says about how identifying it really is, how often it shows up on real websites, and which defenses make a difference. What a browser fingerprint is A fingerprint is a set of facts about your browser and device that, taken together, are rare enough to tell you apart from most other visitors. No single fact is special. Plenty of people use Chrome on Windows with an English interface and a 1920 by 1080 screen. The trick is in the combination. Once you add the time zone, the exact list of fonts, the graphics card and a few dozen other values, the group of browsers that match yours can shrink to one. The attributes fall into two groups. Passive signals These arrive with every request, whether or not a page runs any script. They include your IP address, the User-Agent header that names your browser and operating system, the Accept-Language header that lists your preferred languages, and the other headers your browser sends by default. Our article on the user agent string covers the first of those in detail. Active signals These require JavaScript on the page to go and collect them. Common ones include: Screen and window: resolution, available space, color depth and pixel density. Hardware hints: the number of processor cores and, in some browsers, an approximate amount of memory. Locale: the time zone reported by the system and the date and number formats it uses. Fonts: a script draws the same text in a long list of font names and measures the width of each result. A width that differs from the fallback font means that font is installed. Canvas: the script draws text and shapes into a hidden canvas element and reads the pixels back. Graphics drivers, font rendering and anti-aliasing all leave tiny differences, so the image hashes to a value that varies between machines. WebGL: the 3D graphics interface can report the graphics vendor and renderer, and rendered scenes vary between graphics stacks the same way canvas output does. Audio: the Web Audio API can generate a tone with an oscillator, run it through processing nodes, and hash the output. Differences in audio processing between systems change the result. None of these were designed for tracking. Each exists so that pages can lay themselves out, pick a language or draw graphics. Fingerprinting simply reads them all at once. How unique are browsers, really? Three large studies give a useful picture, and they do not all agree, which is itself informative. The 2010 EFF study Peter Eckersley at the Electronic Frontier Foundation ran the first large experiment through a test site called Panopticlick. Over two weeks it collected roughly 470,000 fingerprints from visitors who chose to take part. 83.6% of them were unique in the sample. Among browsers with Flash or Java installed, which exposed the full list of system fonts, 94.2% were unique. The paper is often credited as the first to use the term browser fingerprinting. The 2016 AmIUnique study Researchers Pierre Laperdrix, Walter Rudametkin and Benoit Baudry collected 118,934 fingerprints over a year through a site called AmIUnique, using 17 attributes including canvas and WebGL. Around 90% of desktop fingerprints were unique. Mobile fingerprints were somewhat less distinctive, but still around 81% unique. The 2018 large-scale study The same research group then partnered with one of the 15 most visited websites in France and analyzed 2,067,942 fingerprints from its ordinary visitors. Only 33.6% were unique. Among mobile visitors, fewer than one in five were. Why the drop? The earlier studies relied on people who went out of their way to visit a privacy test site, and those people tend to run unusual setups. Plugins such as Flash and Java, which leaked a lot, had also largely disappeared by 2018. Writing about the result for Princeton's Center for Information Technology Policy, Arvind Narayanan argued that the early numbers had overstated how well fingerprinting works, and that browsers could realistically reduce it further. The same paper made a less comforting point. Fingerprints that are not unique tend to be fragile. Change a few attributes, by installing a font or updating a driver, and a browser that was hiding in a crowd can become one of a kind. What this means in practice: a third of real visitors being identifiable from their browser alone is a lot less than headlines once suggested, but it is not small. Trackers also rarely rely on the fingerprint alone. They combine it with IP addresses, logins and whatever cookies survive. How common is it on real websites? In 2016, Steven Englehardt and Arvind Narayanan crawled the top one million websites with an instrumented browser. They found canvas fingerprinting on 14,371 sites, served by scripts from about 400 different domains, which works out to nearly 1.5% of the sites they measured. They also found a canvas based font fingerprinting technique on 3,250 sites, and documented audio fingerprinting through the AudioContext interface in the wild for the first time. Fingerprinting is not only used for advertising. Banks and online stores use it to notice when a login comes from an unfamiliar device. Bot detection services use it to tell scripted browsers from real ones. The difficulty for an ordinary visitor is that the same script can serve either purpose, and there is no way to tell from the outside which one it is doing. Why clearing cookies does not help A cookie is something a site stores and reads back. You can see it, delete it, or block it. A fingerprint is computed fresh on every visit from properties the browser already exposes. Deleting cookies, opening a private window or switching to a new browser profile on the same device leaves most of those properties unchanged: the screen, the graphics card, the fonts and the time zone are all still there. That does not make cookie controls pointless. They still stop the easiest and most reliable form of tracking. It just means they are one layer, not the whole defense. What actually reduces fingerprinting Browser makers have settled on two broad strategies, which pull in opposite directions. One makes everyone look the same. The other makes everyone look different every time. Blending in Tor Browser is the clearest example of the first approach. The Tor Project describes it as "specifically engineered to minimize the uniqueness of each user's fingerprint." Its users get the same set of values for as many attributes as possible. Even the window size is controlled: the browser starts with a content area rounded to a multiple of 200 by 100 pixels, and a feature called letterboxing adds margins when the window is resized so the reported size stays in a small number of buckets. The project also explains why it limits user choice, since "any option to choose would only make users more unique." Firefox takes a lighter version of the same path. It blocks scripts from Disconnect's list of known fingerprinters by default, and in private windows or with Enhanced Tracking Protection set to Strict it also limits the information exposed to suspected fingerprinters. Mozilla warns that these protections can occasionally break a site, and that turning protection off for that site fixes it. Randomizing Brave chose the opposite approach in 2020. It adds small amounts of random noise to the output of canvas, WebGL and audio APIs. The changes are invisible to people but change the hash. The important detail is that the noise differs between websites and between browsing sessions, so one site cannot use the value to link you to your activity on another, and a site cannot link today's visit to last week's. Brave's reasoning was that making every browser identical is unrealistic because the fingerprinting surface is so large. Shrinking what browsers reveal The third front is quieter. Browser makers have been reducing the detail they expose by default. Chrome's user agent string no longer carries the full version number or, on Android, the phone model. The W3C publishes guidance for authors of new web standards on how to avoid adding fresh fingerprinting surface in the first place. Blocking the scripts Finally, a tracker blocker that stops known fingerprinting domains from loading prevents the measurement from happening at all on pages that use those services. This does nothing against a site that runs its own fingerprinting code, but it covers the large third-party providers. Things that make you easier to fingerprint Unusual configurations. Rare fonts, a rare screen size or an uncommon language list all narrow the crowd you belong to. Many extensions. Some extensions change pages in ways a script can detect, and a particular combination of them can be distinctive. Inconsistent spoofing. Changing only your user agent can backfire. A browser that claims to be Safari on a Mac while reporting a Windows font list and an Android graphics driver is more unusual than one that tells the truth. Too many tweaks. The Tor Project's point applies everywhere: every setting you change away from the default is another thing that separates you from other people. How to check your own browser You can see what a fingerprinting script sees by visiting a test site. The EFF's Cover Your Tracks, the successor to the original Panopticlick, runs a set of common fingerprinting tests and compares the result with other recent visitors to the site. It reports how many bits of identifying information each attribute carries and whether your overall fingerprint looks unique. AmIUnique, run by the research group behind the 2016 study, does something similar and shows how each value compares with its own dataset. Read the results with the earlier caveat in mind. Visitors to these sites are self-selected and unusually privacy minded, so being unique among them is not the same as being unique among everyone. The useful part is the breakdown. If one attribute, such as a rare font list or an unusual screen size, carries far more information than the rest, that is the thing worth fixing. A practical checklist Keep your browser updated, since vendors keep reducing what they expose. Turn on the anti-tracking features your browser already has before reaching for extra tools. Keep extensions to the ones you actually use. Use separate browser profiles for separate identities. Profiles do not change your hardware fingerprint, but they keep logins and cookies apart, which removes the strongest link between them. If you need a different IP address for one profile, a proxy or VPN handles that part, though it does not change the fingerprint either. Test your setup on EFF's Cover Your Tracks site to see which attributes stand out. A note on Rapid+ Rapid+ Browser includes a built-in ad and tracker blocker that stops requests to known tracking domains, and it keeps each profile's cookies, logins and history separate. It does not claim to make you impossible to fingerprint, and no browser honestly can. You can read about these features on the features page. Sources Eckersley, How Unique Is Your Web Browser? title: Do Ad Blockers Make Pages Load Faster? What the Measurements Show
desc: Ads and trackers are a big share of what many pages download. What researchers measured, how blocking works, and what it costs.
text: The first thing many people notice after turning on an ad and tracker blocker is not the missing ads. It is that pages finish loading sooner and stop jumping around while they do. That impression is backed by measurements, though the size of the effect depends a great deal on the site you are looking at. This article looks at what a typical page actually loads, what researchers measured when they blocked ads and trackers, how blocking works, and what you give up in return. What a modern page actually loads When you open a news article, the article text is usually the smallest part of the job. The page also pulls in scripts, images and frames from other companies: ad networks, analytics services, consent banners, video players, chat widgets and social buttons. These are called third parties, because they come from domains other than the site you visited. The HTTP Archive measures this every year by crawling millions of pages. In its 2024 Web Almanac: 92% of pages loaded at least one third party. The median page among the top thousand websites used 66 different third parties. Across the top million it was 27. Scripts made up the largest share of third-party requests at 30.5%, followed by images at 26.0%. Nearly a third of third parties served advertising, analytics or consent management. Each of those third parties costs something. The browser has to look up a new domain name, open a new connection, download the file, and for scripts, parse and run the code. A script can then load more scripts of its own, so one ad slot can turn into a chain of requests to companies you have never heard of. What happens when one ad loads It helps to follow a single ad slot from start to finish, because the chain is longer than most people expect. The page loads the publisher's ad script, usually from an ad platform's domain. That script often runs an auction. It asks several ad exchanges at once what they will pay to show something to this visitor, sending along whatever it knows about the page and the browser. Each exchange may consult its own partners before answering, which means more requests to more domains. The winning bid returns an ad, which might be an image, a block of HTML or a video player. The ad itself frequently loads more scripts: one to confirm the ad was actually visible, one to count the impression for the advertiser, one or two tracking pixels for audience building. None of this is visible to you. You see one rectangle. Behind it, the browser may have contacted a dozen companies and run several scripts on your phone's processor. Multiply that by the number of ad slots on a long article and the numbers in the Web Almanac start to make sense. What the measurements found The Firefox Tracking Protection study The most cited controlled measurement comes from a 2015 paper by Georgios Kontaxis and Monica Chew, written while Firefox was preparing its Tracking Protection feature. They loaded the 200 most popular news sites, as ranked by Alexa at the time, with and without Tracking Protection, which blocks requests to domains on a list of known trackers. With protection on, they measured: a median 44% reduction in page load time, a median 39% reduction in data used, and a 67.5% reduction in the number of HTTP cookies set during the crawl. Those are medians across sites. Some pages barely changed. Others got dramatically faster. The New York Times mobile test Later that year The New York Times loaded the mobile home pages of 50 news sites with and without an ad blocker and compared the data used. Across the pages tested, more than half of all data came from ads and other content that ad blockers filter out. The results varied widely between sites, which is the same pattern the Firefox study found. Reading these numbers carefully Both studies are from 2015 and focus on news sites, which have always been among the heaviest users of advertising. The web has changed since then. Pages are larger overall, some publishers have trimmed their ad stacks, and browsers have added protections of their own. It would be wrong to promise you a 44% speedup on every site. A page built without heavy advertising, such as a documentation site or a small blog, has little to remove and will load about the same either way. What the research does show, consistently, is that on ad supported pages, third-party advertising and tracking code is a large share of the work, and removing it saves real time and data. Where the time goes Blocking helps in several different ways at once. Fewer network round trips. Every blocked domain is a lookup and a connection that never happens. Less JavaScript on the main thread. Scripts have to be parsed and run on the same thread that responds to your taps and scrolls. On a budget phone this is often a bigger cost than the download itself. Fewer layout jumps. Ads that load late push the text you are reading down the page. Without them, the layout settles sooner. Less data on metered plans. On a prepaid mobile plan, every megabyte of video ad you did not ask for comes out of your allowance. How blocking works Filter lists Most blockers rely on filter lists: large, community maintained collections of rules. Some rules match request addresses, so the browser never sends the request. Others are cosmetic rules that hide the empty boxes and leftover page elements an ad would have filled. Built into the browser Several browsers now block trackers without any extension. Firefox's Enhanced Tracking Protection blocks social media trackers, cross-site tracking cookies, fingerprinters and cryptominers by default. Built-in blocking runs inside the browser itself, so it does not depend on what the extension system allows. At the network level Some people block at the DNS level, with a home server or a filtering DNS service that refuses to resolve known ad domains. This covers every device on the network, including smart TVs and apps. The tradeoff is precision: it can only block whole domains, it cannot hide the empty space an ad leaves behind, and it cannot touch ads served from the same domain as the content. The Chrome extension change Extension based blocking in Chrome changed significantly with Manifest V3. The older extension platform let blockers inspect each request with the webRequest API and decide whether to cancel it. Manifest V3 moves that decision into the browser through a declarative rules system. Google's published timeline shows Manifest V2 extensions disabled for all Chrome users from Chrome 138 in July 2025, after a gradual rollout that began in late 2024. The most popular blocker, uBlock Origin, depended on the older API. Its author released a separate Manifest V3 version, uBlock Origin Lite, and its FAQ explains some of the limits: the declarative system cannot enforce rules according to the address shown in the address bar, so certain capabilities of the original cannot be carried over. The tradeoffs Some sites break Blocking a script a page depends on can break a login button, a video player or a checkout. Mozilla notes that its Strict tracking protection mode may cause breakage on some sites. Every good blocker lets you switch it off for a single site, and that is usually the fix. Publishers lose income Much of the free web is paid for by advertising. If you rely on a site, consider allowing it in your blocker or supporting it directly. Blocking trackers while allowing ordinary ads is a reasonable middle ground on sites you want to support. Blockers are only as good as their lists New ad and tracking domains appear all the time. A blocker with stale lists catches less, and a first-party tracker served from the site's own domain may slip through any list based approach. Why phones feel it most On a fast laptop with a wired connection, a page full of trackers might load in a second or two either way, and the difference is easy to miss. On a mid-range phone on a weak mobile signal, the same page has a slower processor running the scripts and a slower, less reliable network fetching them. Every extra connection costs more time, and every script takes longer to run while the page stays unresponsive. The same blocklist that saves a fraction of a second on a desktop can save several seconds on a phone, along with a noticeable share of a small data allowance. Choosing a blocker A few questions separate a good choice from a poor one: Who maintains the lists, and how often are they updated? A blocker is only as current as its rules. Can you turn it off for one site in a couple of taps? You will need this sooner or later. Does it block trackers as well as ads? For speed and privacy, the tracking scripts matter as much as the ads themselves. Does it depend on an extension platform that may change? The Chrome change above is a reminder that extension capabilities are decided by the browser maker. What does the blocker itself collect? Some extensions have been sold or changed hands over the years. Prefer ones with a clear owner and a clear privacy policy, or blocking built into a browser you already trust. How to measure it yourself You do not have to take anyone's word for it. In a desktop browser: Open the developer tools and switch to the Network panel. Tick the option to disable the cache, so every load starts from scratch. Load a page with your blocker switched off for that site and note the number of requests, the amount transferred and the finish time shown at the bottom of the panel. Turn the blocker back on, reload, and compare. Repeat a few times, since network conditions vary from one load to the next. Try a news site, a recipe site and a site with no ads at all. The differences between those three tell you more than any average. A note on Rapid+ Rapid+ Browser has an ad and tracker blocker built into the browser on both Android and Windows, so it does not depend on extension APIs. It blocks requests to known ad and tracking domains before they are sent, and Rapid+ itself collects no analytics from the app. You can read more on the features page. title: Proxy vs VPN: What Each One Actually Hides
desc: Both put another server between you and the web. They cover different traffic, protect it differently, and hide different things from different people.
text: A proxy and a VPN both put another computer between you and the websites you visit. That shared idea is why people use the two words as if they meant the same thing, and why some apps sell a plain proxy with a "VPN" label on it. They are not the same. The difference decides which of your traffic gets rerouted, whether anyone on your network can read it, and who ends up holding the list of sites you visit. This guide walks through how each one works at the network level, what each one hides and from whom, and when you would pick one over the other. The short version A proxy is something a single app is told to use. Your browser sends its requests to the proxy, the proxy talks to the website, and the website sees the proxy's IP address instead of yours. Apps that are not configured to use it keep connecting directly, as if the proxy did not exist. A VPN works one layer lower, inside the operating system. It creates a virtual network interface and routes traffic from every app on the device through an encrypted tunnel to the VPN server. Your browser, your mail client and the game updating in the background all leave through the same exit. Proxy (HTTP or SOCKS5) VPN What it covers Only apps set up to use it Traffic from the whole device, unless split tunneling is on Encryption to the server None of its own Yes, that is the purpose of the tunnel What the website sees The proxy's IP address The VPN server's IP address What your Wi-Fi or ISP sees The proxy's address, and usually the names of the sites you request through it One encrypted connection to the VPN server Where DNS lookups happen Depends on settings, often still on your own resolver Inside the tunnel, if the VPN is configured properly Typical setup A host, a port, and sometimes a username and password An app or a system profile from the provider How a proxy server works A proxy is a server that makes connections on a client's behalf. Your browser opens a connection to the proxy and asks it to reach a particular site. The proxy connects from its own address and passes data back and forth. MDN's guide to proxy servers separates the two directions you will see described: a forward proxy sits in front of clients, which is the kind you type into browser settings, while a reverse proxy sits in front of servers, the way a content delivery network does. The two forward proxy types you will meet most often are HTTP proxies and SOCKS5 proxies. They solve the same problem in different ways, and the differences matter. HTTP proxies and the CONNECT method An HTTP proxy speaks HTTP. When you load a plain http:// page through it, the browser hands the proxy the full request: the address, the headers, any cookies and any form data. The proxy reads all of it, fetches the page and returns the response. It can log that content, cache it, or change it before you see it. This is the main reason open proxies copied from public lists are a bad idea for anything that matters. You are giving a stranger a seat in the middle of your traffic. HTTPS works differently. For an https:// address the browser sends the proxy a short request such as CONNECT example.com:443. The HTTP specification defines this method in RFC 9110: the proxy opens a TCP connection to that host and from then on relays bytes in both directions without interpreting them. The browser then performs its TLS handshake with the real website through that tunnel. The result is that the proxy knows which host you asked for, when, and roughly how much data moved. It cannot read the pages, your passwords or your cookies, because those are encrypted between your browser and the website. An HTTP proxy is a reasonable tool for HTTPS browsing as long as you accept that its operator learns which sites you visit. SOCKS5 SOCKS is older and more general. Version 5 is defined in RFC 1928, published in 1996. A SOCKS server does not care which application protocol you speak. It relays TCP connections, and version 5 added a way to relay UDP as well through a command called UDP ASSOCIATE. The client tells the server which address and port it wants, the server connects, and after that it simply forwards data. Two details in the specifications matter in day to day use. First, SOCKS5 has no encryption of its own. The protocol negotiates how to authenticate and where to connect, nothing more. The most common login method, username and password, is defined in RFC 1929, and that document is blunt about it: the request "carries the password in cleartext," so the method is "not recommended for environments where 'sniffing' is possible and practical." If you use a password protected SOCKS5 proxy across the open internet, anyone on the path between you and that proxy can read the password. Second, a SOCKS5 request can name the destination either as an IP address or as a domain name. When the client sends the name, the proxy performs the DNS lookup. When the client resolves the name itself and sends only the IP address, the lookup happens on your own connection. That choice has real consequences. Where your DNS lookups happen Before a browser can connect anywhere it has to turn a name like example.com into an IP address. If that lookup goes to your usual resolver, which is often run by your internet provider, the provider still receives a list of every domain you visit, proxy or no proxy. Firefox exposes this as its own checkbox, "Proxy DNS when using SOCKS v5," backed by the network.proxy.socks_remote_dns preference. Mozilla's enterprise policy documentation lists the same switch as UseProxyForDNS. The command line tool curl makes the same distinction in its proxy schemes: socks5:// resolves names locally, while socks5h:// hands the name to the proxy. If the point of your SOCKS5 setup is to keep your browsing away from your provider, check that name lookups go through it too. How a VPN works A VPN, or virtual private network, adds a virtual network adapter to your device. The operating system routes traffic into that adapter, the VPN software encrypts it and sends it to the VPN server, and the server decrypts it and forwards it to the internet. Replies come back the same way. Common protocols include WireGuard, OpenVPN and IPsec. They differ in speed and design, but all of them encrypt the traffic between your device and the server. The Electronic Frontier Foundation's Surveillance Self-Defense guide puts it plainly: a VPN "routes all your web traffic through an 'encrypted tunnel' between your devices and the VPN server," and it "hides your outgoing traffic from your ISP and the local network owner." That second part is the main thing a VPN gives you that a basic proxy does not. The same guide is just as clear about the limits. Your browsing becomes visible to the VPN provider instead of your ISP, and "a VPN is not a tool for anonymity," because cookies, logins and fingerprinting can still identify you to the sites you visit. A VPN label is not a guarantee A VPN is only as trustworthy as the company that runs it and the app you install. In a 2016 study, researchers from CSIRO and partner institutions examined 283 Android apps that request the system VPN permission. 18% of them used tunneling protocols with no encryption at all, around 84% leaked IPv6 traffic outside the tunnel, and 66% leaked DNS traffic. Apps have improved since then, but the lesson still applies. The word on the label tells you nothing about how the app actually behaves. Who sees what The clearest way to compare the two is to go through each party that could be watching and ask what they learn. The website you visit With either one, the site sees the IP address of the proxy or VPN server instead of yours. That changes the location the site guesses for you and keeps your home connection out of its logs. It does not change anything else. If you are signed in, the site knows who you are. Cookies from earlier visits still identify you. Your browser's fingerprint is identical. Our guide to browser fingerprinting explains how much a site can learn with no cookies at all. Your Wi-Fi network and internet provider This is where the two really diverge. With an unencrypted proxy, whoever runs the café Wi-Fi, and your ISP, can see that you are connecting to the proxy. They can usually also see where you are asking it to go, because the destination travels in the clear, either in the CONNECT line of an HTTP proxy or inside the SOCKS request. For HTTPS sites they still cannot read the pages. For plain HTTP sites they can read everything. With a working VPN they see an encrypted stream to one server and nothing about what is inside it. There is a useful middle ground. OpenSSH's -D option makes ssh listen on a local port and "act as a SOCKS server," forwarding each connection over the encrypted SSH channel. Point your browser at that local port and the hop from your device to the SSH server is encrypted, so the local network sees only an SSH connection. You get proxy behavior for the apps you choose, with the network protection of a VPN. The proxy or VPN operator Both see the destinations of everything you send through them. A VPN operator sees this for every app on the device, not only the browser. Neither can read HTTPS content. Both can log timing, volume and destinations, and both can be compelled to hand those records over. The EFF guide notes that VPN providers receive law enforcement requests like anyone else, and that many keep as much information as ISPs do. Your other apps A proxy configured in the browser does nothing for other apps. Your mail client, messengers and system updates keep using your normal connection. Sometimes that is exactly what you want. Sometimes it is a leak you did not notice. When a proxy is the better choice You want routing per app or per profile. A proxy lets one browser profile appear to come from another country while everything else on the device, your banking app included, stays on your real connection. You need to see a site the way another region sees it. Developers, marketers and support staff do this constantly to check regional pricing, language redirects and geo restrictions. Your school or employer provides one. Many organizations require browser traffic to pass through an authenticated HTTP proxy. You already have a server. Any machine you can SSH into becomes a SOCKS5 proxy with a single command, and nothing extra needs to be installed on it. You care about overhead. A proxy adds no encryption layer of its own, so it asks less of the battery and processor on older phones. When a VPN is the better choice You are on a network you do not trust. Hotel and café Wi-Fi is the classic case. A VPN hides your traffic from whoever runs it. You want every app covered. Plenty of apps have no proxy setting at all. You want destinations hidden from your ISP. A plain proxy leaves them visible on the wire. You can also use both. A browser profile pointed at a proxy, on a device connected to a VPN, sends that profile's traffic into the VPN tunnel first and then out through the proxy. Mistakes worth avoiding Treating either one as anonymity Changing your IP address hides one signal out of many. A logged in account, a saved cookie or a distinctive browser fingerprint links your visits together regardless of the exit address. Using random free proxies An open proxy from a public list belongs to someone you know nothing about. For HTTP pages it can read and alter everything you send and receive. Even for HTTPS it learns every site you visit. If you would not hand a stranger your browsing history, do not route your browser through one. Forgetting DNS and IPv6 A SOCKS5 proxy without remote DNS still tells your resolver every domain you look up. On the VPN side, the leaks found in the Android study were mostly DNS and IPv6 traffic slipping around the tunnel. After changing anything, load a DNS leak test page and confirm the results match what you expect. Sending proxy passwords in the clear SOCKS5 username and password authentication is not encrypted. For a proxy you reach over the internet, wrap it in SSH or use a provider that offers an encrypted connection. A note on Rapid+ Rapid+ Browser has a proxy mode for HTTP and SOCKS5 that you set separately for each profile, with an optional username and password and a test button that checks the connection before you rely on it. It does not supply proxy servers. It connects to the one you choose. The details are on the proxy browser page.
