title: Separate Browser Profiles for Work, Personal and Shopping: Why They Work
desc: One browser, several separate lives. How profiles keep logins and cookies apart, what they do not protect, and how to set them up well.
text: Most people run their whole online life through one browser window. Work email sits next to personal email, the shopping site remembers last week's search, and every service you are signed into shares the same store of cookies. Browser profiles split that into separate spaces, each with its own logins, history and saved data. It is one of the simplest improvements you can make to both privacy and daily sanity, and every major browser already has it. What a profile actually separates A profile is a separate set of browser data kept in its own folder on your device. Google's help page for Chrome sums it up in one line: "With profiles, you can keep all your Chrome info separate, like bookmarks, history, passwords, and other settings." Apple's documentation for Safari, which added profiles in Safari 17, is more specific. Each profile has its own history, cookies, website data, extensions, Tab Groups and favorites. Extensions are installed once but switched on or off per profile, and new profiles start with them off. When you delete a profile, its history, cookies and website data go with it. The details vary between browsers, but the core is the same everywhere: cookies and site storage in one profile are invisible to the others. That one property is what makes profiles useful. Why cookies make this matter Cookies are small pieces of data a site asks your browser to store and send back with later requests. The cookie standard, RFC 6265, ties each cookie to the site that set it. That is how a site keeps you logged in: it hands your browser a session cookie, and every request after that carries the cookie back. Inside one profile, this means every tab that opens a given site shares the same login. If you are signed into one account, you are signed in everywhere in that profile. Want to use a second account on the same service at the same time? Most sites either do not allow it or make you juggle an account switcher. What browsers already do for third-party cookies For years, the bigger privacy problem was third-party cookies. An advertising network embedded on thousands of sites could set one cookie and read it back on every one of those sites, building a picture of your browsing. Browsers have since cut this down with storage partitioning. MDN explains that Firefox now "double-keys all client-side state by the origin of the resource being loaded and by the top-level site," so an embedded tracker gets a different storage area on each website it appears on. Mozilla turned this on for all desktop Firefox users in June 2022 under the name Total Cookie Protection, describing it as a separate "cookie jar" for every website you visit. Partitioning is a real improvement, but it solves a different problem. It stops one site's embedded tracker from following you to another site. It does nothing about the cookies of the sites you visit directly, which is exactly where your logins, carts and recommendations live. If you want your work account and your personal account kept apart, or your gift shopping kept off the family computer's main profile, partitioning will not do it. Separate profiles will. Profiles, private windows and containers Three features get confused with each other. They solve different problems. Private window Firefox container Profile Separate cookies and site data Yes, temporary Yes Yes Kept after you close it No Yes Yes Separate history Not saved at all No, shared Yes Separate extensions and settings No No, shared Yes Good for A one-off session you want forgotten Several accounts side by side in one window Long-term separate identities A private window is a throwaway profile. It is perfect for checking something without leaving a trace in your main history, but you cannot keep a login in it, because everything is discarded when you close it. Firefox's Multi-Account Containers extension gives each container its own storage, such as cookies and localStorage, so tabs in different containers can be signed into different accounts on the same site. All containers still live inside one Firefox profile, so bookmarks, extensions and the history list are shared. A profile is the most complete of the three. It keeps nearly everything apart, and it stays that way until you delete it. Where profiles earn their keep Work and personal accounts This is the classic case. Your work email, calendar and documents live in one profile. Your personal accounts live in another. You never send a work file from the wrong account, your personal bookmarks do not end up in front of a colleague during a screen share, and logging out of one does not log you out of the other. Shopping and research Shopping sites and their partners are among the heaviest users of tracking and personalization. Keeping that activity in its own profile means the recommendations and ads that follow your shopping stay in that profile, instead of appearing in the browser you use for everything else. Shared devices On a family tablet or laptop, a profile per person keeps each person's accounts, history and saved passwords out of the others' way. It is not a security wall against someone determined, but it prevents the everyday accidents. Clients and side projects Freelancers and agency staff often keep one profile per client, each signed into that client's accounts. Switching clients means switching profiles, not signing out of a dozen services. Testing and troubleshooting A clean profile with no extensions and no saved data is the quickest way to tell whether a broken site is broken for everyone or only for your setup. Pairing a profile with its own network settings Some browsers let a profile carry its own proxy or user agent. That turns a profile into a complete separate identity: its own logins, its own exit IP address and its own reported device, while your other profiles stay on your normal connection. A sample setup Here is a layout that works for a lot of people, to make the idea concrete. Profile Signed into Kept here Left out Work Work email, calendar, company tools Work bookmarks, the password manager your employer requires Personal social accounts, personal extensions Personal Personal email, banking, family photos Everyday bookmarks, your own password manager Shopping sites, random sign-ups Shopping and sign-ups Store accounts, newsletters, coupon sites Order tracking pages, wish lists Email and banking The rule of thumb is that each profile has one job. When you sign up for something new, ask which profile it belongs to before you create the account. That one habit does most of the work. Profiles and sync In browsers with a sync account, sync is usually tied to the profile, not to the whole browser. That is a feature. Your work profile can sync to a work account and your personal profile to a personal one, so bookmarks and passwords never cross between them, even on another computer. It also means a mistake carries over. If you sign your personal sync account into the work profile, your personal passwords and history arrive there on every device you use. Check which account each profile is synced to when you set it up, and again after reinstalling. What profiles do not do Profiles separate stored data. They do not change the device underneath, and that has consequences. Your fingerprint is the same. Every profile on a device shares the same screen, graphics hardware, fonts and time zone. A site that uses browser fingerprinting could recognize two profiles as the same machine. Your IP address is the same, unless you give a profile its own proxy or route it through a VPN. They are not a security boundary. Malware on the device, or anyone with access to your user account, can reach every profile's files. They do not lock by default. In most browsers anyone using the computer can open any profile. Some browsers add a lock, but check before you rely on it. Setting them up well Give each profile a clear name and color. The point is to always know which one you are in. A colored icon in the toolbar is enough. Start with two or three. Work, personal and one for shopping or experiments covers most people. Too many and you will stop using them consistently. Keep extensions minimal in each. An extension you need for work does not have to run while you shop. Lock the sensitive one. If your browser supports a lock per profile, use it for the profile that holds banking or work accounts. Decide where links open. Links from other apps usually open in the last used profile. Know which one that is. Mistakes that undo the benefit Signing in from the wrong profile The most common slip is clicking a link from an email or chat app, having it open in whichever profile was used last, and signing in there without noticing. The account is now in two profiles. Glance at the profile color before you type a password. Saving passwords everywhere When the browser offers to save a password, it saves it into the current profile. Saving the same password in several profiles spreads it around and defeats part of the separation. Save each login once, in the profile it belongs to. Making too many A profile per website is not organization, it is clutter. If you have to think about which profile to open, you will eventually stop opening the right one. What about phones? Profiles grew up as a desktop feature, and on phones the picture is patchier. Mobile browsers vary a lot here: some have no profiles at all, some offer only a separate private mode, and a few support several full profiles. Many people fall back on using two different browser apps, one for work and one for personal use, which gives the same separation at the cost of two sets of settings to maintain. If your phone is where most of your browsing happens, check what your mobile browser actually supports before building a habit around it. Cleaning up Deleting a profile is the cleanest reset a browser offers. Google's help page notes that when you delete a Chrome profile, "the profile's bookmarks, history, passwords, and other settings are erased from the computer." Apple says deleting a Safari profile removes its history, cookies and website data. That makes a throwaway profile useful for short projects: use it for a few weeks, export anything you need to keep, then delete it and everything it collected goes with it. A note on Rapid+ Profiles are at the center of Rapid+ Browser. Each profile has its own tabs, logins, cookies, history, bookmarks, saved passwords, proxy and settings, and you can switch between them in one tap. On Android a profile can be locked with your fingerprint or face, and on Windows with a PIN. The multiple profiles page has the details. title: What Is a User Agent String, and Why Do Websites Care?
desc: Your browser names five other browsers every time it loads a page. The reason is thirty years of browsers pretending to be each other.
text: Every request your browser makes carries a short line of text describing the software that sent it. In Chrome on Windows it reads something like this: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/143.0.0.0 Safari/537.36 That line mentions Mozilla, AppleWebKit, KHTML, Gecko, Chrome and Safari. You are using one browser. This is the user agent string, and the clutter inside it is the result of three decades of browsers pretending to be one another so that websites would treat them properly. Here is where it came from, what sites actually do with it, why browser makers have started freezing it, and when changing it is useful. What the user agent string is HTTP, the protocol every web page travels over, lets a client describe itself in a User-Agent request header. The current HTTP specification, RFC 9110, defines the header, and MDN describes it as "a characteristic string that lets servers and network peers identify the application, operating system, vendor, and/or version of the requesting user agent." The same value is available to scripts on the page through navigator.userAgent. So a site can read it both on its server, when the request arrives, and in the browser, after the page loads. For web browsers MDN gives the usual shape as: Mozilla/5.0 (<system-information>) <platform> (<platform-details>) <extensions> How it got so strange The best known telling of this history is a 2008 post by Aaron Andersen on the WebAIM blog. The short version goes like this. Early browsers named themselves honestly. NCSA Mosaic sent NCSA_Mosaic/2.0 (Windows 3.1). Then Netscape arrived. Its internal name was Mozilla, which the WebAIM post explains as short for "Mosaic Killer," and it identified itself as Mozilla/1.0. Netscape supported frames and Mosaic did not, so web developers started checking the user agent and sending framed pages only to browsers that said "Mozilla." When Internet Explorer arrived it also supported frames, but it was not Mozilla, so it got the plain version. Microsoft's answer was to make Internet Explorer say it was "Mozilla compatible," with strings like Mozilla/1.22 (compatible; MSIE 2.0; Windows 95). That pattern repeated for every new engine: The Mozilla project's Gecko engine, which later powered Firefox, used Mozilla/5.0 plus a Gecko/ token, and sites began checking for Gecko. Konqueror's KHTML engine was not Gecko, so it added (KHTML, like Gecko) to receive the same pages. Apple built Safari on KHTML, forked it into WebKit, and kept the "like Gecko" wording so sites written for KHTML kept working. Google's Chrome used WebKit and kept the Safari tokens too. Each browser inherited the previous browser's disguise and added its own name at the end. MDN's summary of the first token is dry but accurate: "For historical reasons, almost every browser today sends it." Reading a modern user agent Take the Chrome string from the top of this article apart, piece by piece: Token What it means Mozilla/5.0 Historical compatibility claim. Carries no real information. (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) Operating system and architecture. Windows 11 still reports itself as NT 10.0. AppleWebKit/537.36 Engine family. Chrome's Blink engine was forked from WebKit, and this version number has stayed fixed for years. (KHTML, like Gecko) Inherited compatibility claim from the KHTML days. Chrome/143.0.0.0 The actual browser and major version. The trailing zeros are deliberate. Safari/537.36 Another compatibility claim, so sites checking for Safari still serve WebKit friendly code. Firefox is shorter, and still carries its own fossil: a fixed Gecko/20100101 build date. Safari on a Mac reports a version token such as Version/26.0 next to a macOS version of 10_15_7, a number that no longer changes with the real operating system. Chrome on Android now reports something like (Linux; Android 10; K), where the Android version is fixed and the phone model has been replaced by a single letter. What websites do with it Sites read the user agent for a handful of reasons, some sensible and some not. Choosing a mobile or desktop page Many sites still decide between a phone layout and a desktop layout on the server. MDN's advice for this case is simple: look for the string Mobi anywhere in the user agent, and serve the desktop site when it is absent. Offering the right download Software sites read the operating system to put the right installer at the top of the page. It is a convenience, and it is why a download page sometimes guesses wrong when you have changed your user agent. Counting visitors Analytics tools group visits by browser and operating system so site owners know what to test against. Blocking or warning Some sites show an "unsupported browser" banner, or refuse to load at all, when they do not recognize the name in the string. Bot filters also look at it, since badly written scrapers often send an empty or obviously fake value. Guessing at features The worst use is deciding which features a browser supports from its name. MDN warns that parsing the user agent this way "is very hard to do reliably, and is often a cause of bugs," partly because browsers "routinely pretend to be another browser." Its example is a site that checks for the word "Chrome" before using a JavaScript feature. That check wrongly includes older Chrome versions and other Chromium based browsers, and wrongly excludes any other browser that adds the feature later. The recommended alternative is feature detection: test whether the feature exists, and use a fallback if it does not. Not just browsers Anything that speaks HTTP sends a user agent, and the ones outside browsers are often more honest. The command line tool curl, for instance, sends curl/ followed by its version number unless you tell it otherwise. Its manual notes that the header can be replaced with any value, or removed entirely by passing an empty one. Search engine crawlers identify themselves too. Google's crawler includes the word Googlebot in its user agent, and many sites treat it differently from ordinary visitors, since being crawled properly affects how they appear in search. That creates an obvious incentive to lie, and Google's own documentation addresses it. It describes "spammers or other troublemakers" accessing sites "while claiming to be from Google," and tells site owners to check the visitor's IP address instead: run a reverse DNS lookup, confirm the name ends in googlebot.com, google.com or googleusercontent.com, then run a forward lookup on that name and confirm it returns the original address. That advice sums up the user agent's place on the web. It is a useful hint that the client chooses to send. It is not proof of anything. Why browsers are freezing it A long, detailed user agent is useful for fingerprinting, since it adds identifying detail to every request without a single line of script. MDN notes that this "historically raised privacy concerns" and that supporting browsers now provide "a reduced set of information" in the header and in related JavaScript properties. Chrome made the biggest change. The Chromium project's User-Agent Reduction plan rolled out in stages: Chrome 101: the minor version became 0.0.0. Chrome 107: the reduced desktop string rolled out. Chrome 110: the reduced Android string rolled out, with the fixed Android 10 and the model replaced by K. Chrome 113: the last opt-out ended and every page load received the reduced string. The operating system tokens have been frozen too. Microsoft states that user agent strings "won't be updated to differentiate between Windows 11 and Windows 10," which is why both report Windows NT 10.0. User-Agent Client Hints The information did not disappear. It moved behind a request. Under the User-Agent Client Hints proposal, browsers that support it send only a few low detail values by default, in headers such as Sec-CH-UA and Sec-CH-UA-Platform. A server that needs more asks for it with an Accept-CH response header, and the browser includes the requested values on later requests. Scripts can do the same through navigator.userAgentData.getHighEntropyValues(). Microsoft's documentation shows how this works for the Windows question: a Sec-CH-UA-Platform-Version value of 13.0.0 or higher means Windows 11. It also lists which browsers support it at all. Edge, Chrome and Opera do. Firefox does not, so a site using Client Hints alone cannot tell which Windows version a Firefox user is on. How to see your own The quickest way is to open your browser's developer tools, switch to the Console, type navigator.userAgent and press Enter. The string your browser reports to scripts appears straight away. To see the header itself, open the Network panel, reload the page, click the first request and look under Request Headers. In browsers that support Client Hints you will see the Sec-CH-UA headers listed there as well, and you can compare how much each one reveals. Doing this once is worth it. It makes the freezing described above concrete: the version number ends in zeros, and on Windows 11 the operating system still reads as NT 10.0. When changing your user agent helps Most browsers can send a different user agent, either through a "desktop site" option, through developer tools, or through a dedicated switcher. There are good reasons to do it: Getting the full desktop site on a phone, when the mobile version hides a feature you need. Testing, to see how your own site responds to an iPhone or an older browser without owning one. Getting past lazy blocking, on sites that turn away browsers they do not recognize even though the browser would work fine. It also has limits that are easy to forget: It does not change your engine. Claiming to be Safari does not make your browser render like Safari. If a site sends code tailored to the browser it thinks you are, things can break. It does not hide you. The user agent is one attribute among dozens. A string that does not match your other signals, such as a desktop Mac claim from a touch screen device with an Android graphics driver, can make you stand out more. Our guide to browser fingerprinting explains why. Client Hints and scripts can still see the truth. If your browser sends Client Hints, or a page checks other properties, the disguise may only cover the header. A sensible habit is to change the user agent only where you need it, rather than everywhere. Keeping it per profile works well: one browser profile set to a desktop identity for a stubborn site, and your everyday profile left at the default. A note on Rapid+ Rapid+ Browser has a built-in user agent switcher with presets for Chrome, Firefox and Safari on a computer and for several iPhone models, plus a custom option where you can type any string. The choice is saved per profile, so one profile can use a desktop identity while the others stay at the default. See the user agent switcher page for details.
